scenes.visual_overview: Compare Standard-IA with One Zone-IA for rarely read data where instant retrieval is still necessary.

scenes.visual_example: A media company stores older production files in multi-AZ Standard-IA, but reproducible secondary copies could use One Zone-IA.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Cheaper storage trades off availability-zone resilience and adds retrieval and minimum-duration charges.
scenes.narration: This slide compares two lower-cost S3 classes that both retain millisecond retrieval. Look first at the blue Standard-IA panel. The AWS Region diagram shows copies across three Availability Zones; this is suitable for rarely used production files that still need multi-zone resilience. Now move right to One Zone-IA. The purple illustration contains data only in AZ one, while the other two zones show no copy. That lower price comes with a real risk: destruction of that zone can destroy the only copy. Both panels mention a 30-day minimum storage duration. The row underneath adds two costs that are easy to miss: retrieval charges for reading data and a pro-rated charge if you delete before the minimum billing period. A 30-day billing minimum does not make deletion impossible. In the worked media-company example, older project files that must survive AZ failure go to Standard-IA; an extra copy that can be reproduced from another source might go to One Zone-IA. The exam cue reinforces the trade-off. When the question says infrequent access plus rapid reads, check whether the data must survive an AZ failure before choosing a class.

scenes.title: S3 Glacier Storage Classes
scenes.visual_overview: Compare three archive tiers by retrieval time, minimum duration and retrieval charges.
visual_walkthrough: Glacier Instant: millisecond reads, 90-day minimum
Glacier Flexible: expedited 1–5 min, standard 3–5 h, bulk 5–12 h, 90 days
Deep Archive: standard ~12 h, bulk ~48 h, 180 days
Three-column comparison of retrieval charges including Flexible bulk free
Bottom decision sequence and matching archive, DR and compliance examples
scenes.visual_example: Media archives that still require immediate reading use Glacier Instant, restore-based backups use Flexible, and rarely retrieved compliance records use Deep Archive.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The word Glacier does not imply identical restore time, retrieval pricing or minimum duration.
scenes.narration: This slide teaches three archive classes through a side-by-side retrieval comparison. The left blue mountain is S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: use it for data that is seldom read but must open in milliseconds, with a 90-day minimum billing duration. In the purple middle card, Glacier Flexible Retrieval needs a restore. The labels distinguish expedited at roughly one to five minutes when capacity permits, standard around three to five hours and bulk around five to twelve hours. Its minimum storage duration is also 90 days; the lower table notes Flexible bulk retrieval is free, while other modes can charge. The gold right card is Glacier Deep Archive: the cheapest storage of these three for very long retention, with standard retrieval around twelve hours, bulk around forty-eight hours and a 180-day minimum. These times are typical service modes, not a promise of an exact completion time. Follow the bottom decision strip: ask how soon the data is needed, select a class that meets that deadline, then account for minimum duration and retrieval costs. The worked examples match occasional instant-read media to Instant, disaster recovery that can wait to Flexible, and rarely opened compliance records to Deep Archive. The overall lesson is to choose by retrieval behavior first, then optimize cost.

scenes.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
scenes.visual_overview: How S3 automatically moves eligible objects across access tiers while optional archive modes add restore requirements.
visual_walkthrough: Unknown access pattern bucket enters monitoring panel and per-object fee
Automatic Frequent, Infrequent after 30 days and Archive Instant after 90 days
Optional Archive Access from 90 and Deep Archive Access from 180 days require restore
Return arrows and <128KB exception
Lower example of new reports becoming infrequently used
scenes.visual_example: New reports begin Frequent Access; after 30 unused days eligible data moves to Infrequent and after 90 to Archive Instant, with optional longer archive settings.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The first three tiers support millisecond reads; optional deep archive tiers require restores and explicit enablement.
scenes.narration: This diagram explains the difference between following a fixed age-based Lifecycle rule and letting S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitor real use. Start at the green bucket on the left: an organization uploads reports without knowing which ones will stay popular. The purple panel shows S3 monitoring object access and moving eligible objects automatically, with a small per-object monitoring cost. Trace the five buckets to the right. New objects begin in Frequent Access; after thirty consecutive days without access, eligible objects enter Infrequent Access; after ninety consecutive days, they can enter Archive Instant Access. All three automatic tiers retain millisecond reads. The dashed boxes mark optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access. These must be enabled and require a restore when data is brought back; the slide shows configurable thresholds starting at ninety and one hundred eighty days respectively. The arrows underneath indicate movement as access patterns change, not a one-way mandatory migration through every tier. The small note makes an important exception: objects smaller than 128 kilobytes stay in the Frequent Access tier without monitoring fees. At the bottom, follow the reports example from actively viewed to rarely used. Intelligent-Tiering reduces the effort of guessing future access, but it does not eliminate all storage and archival costs.

scenes.visual_overview: A single comparison matrix lets you choose among all major S3 classes using four decision axes.

Four data rows: access, AZ design, retrieval wait, minimum storage duration
Intelligent-Tiering optional archive restore exception
Four-step lower decision guide
Training dataset example recommends Standard
scenes.visual_example: Frequently accessed model training datasets requiring immediate multi-AZ availability map to S3 Standard.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose class from access, zone resilience, retrieval deadline and minimum billed duration; no one class wins every requirement.
scenes.narration: The purpose of this slide is to put the earlier storage lessons into one exam decision table. Do not read it as a sequence of stages: each vertical column is a competing option. Scan the first row for access frequency. Standard is frequent; Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are infrequent; Glacier tiers are archival; and Intelligent-Tiering changes placement as access patterns change. Now read across the Availability Zone row. Everything shown is multi-zone except One Zone-IA, which stores data in one zone. Move down to retrieval time. Standard, the IA classes, the three automatic Intelligent-Tiering tiers and Glacier Instant all support millisecond reads. Glacier Flexible needs minutes to hours, and Deep Archive generally needs hours. Optional Intelligent-Tiering archive modes also require a restore. The last row shows minimum storage duration charges: none for Standard or the Intelligent-Tiering class, thirty days for IA, ninety for Glacier Instant and Flexible, and one hundred eighty for Deep Archive. The four boxes along the bottom turn this table into a practical method: assess access pattern, decide AZ resilience, check retrieval deadline, and verify duration charges. The worked training-dataset example requires frequent immediate access across AZs, so Standard is the correct selection. The grid teaches trade-offs, not a universal cheapest class.

scenes.title: Storage Pricing: Cost Drivers
scenes.visual_overview: S3 costs include more than GB stored, illustrated by active training, occasional backups and long-term archives.
visual_walkthrough: Left-to-right Standard, Infrequent Access and Glacier Deep Archive lifecycle comparison
Right sidebar: GB-month, request, retrieval, minimum duration, monitoring, transfer
Worked table of three datasets with recommended class and charging differences
Exam cue reminds to calculate combined cost categories
scenes.visual_example: Active training uses Standard, monthly backup uses Infrequent Access, annual archive uses Deep Archive.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Lower storage cost per GB-month can be offset by request/retrieval charges, minimum duration and transfer.
scenes.narration: This visual is about calculating total storage economics rather than selecting the lowest advertised price per gigabyte. Begin with the three storage boxes across the top. Active ML training files are read and written frequently, so S3 Standard often makes sense despite a higher GB-month storage rate. An infrequent backup can move to Standard-IA and pay less for storage, but reads and early deletion can cost extra. A very long-term archive can move to Glacier Deep Archive for the lowest storage rate, with much slower restoration and a longer minimum charge. The arrows indicate a possible evolution of data; a team would configure suitable Lifecycle transitions where appropriate. Next, read the cost-driver column on the right. Storage is billed by quantity over time. PUT, GET and other requests can add charges. Infrequent and archival retrievals can cost money; minimum duration floors, Intelligent-Tiering monitoring and data transfer can also affect the total. Now inspect the worked table at the bottom: active training, monthly backups and annual archival access each have a different recommended class and cost profile. The exam cue is about adding all those factors, not just comparing one storage rate. Actual AWS prices vary by Region and operation, so the illustrated categories guide an estimate rather than supply a fixed quote.
